item.title: Italy October preliminary CPI +5.4% vs +4.6% y/y expected
item.description:
• Prior +4.2%
  • HICP +5.6% vs +4.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.2%

Inflation accelerated sharply in October 2026, but the increase was primarily driven by energy prices, with both regulated and non-regulated energy products recording significant increases. Regulated energy inflation surged from 25.8% to 59.5% y/y, while non-regulated energy prices accelerated from 22.5% to 29.4%. Higher energy costs remain the dominant driver of the inflationary shock.

However, price pressures were not limited to energy. Unprocessed food inflation accelerated from 5.5% to 7.5%, while processed food prices also returned to positive annual growth. Services inflation picked up more modestly, rising to 2.9% from 2.6%, with transport-related services accelerating to 3.1%.

The goods component was particularly notable, with annual inflation jumping to 7.5% from 5.4%, while services inflation remained considerably more contained. This suggests that the latest acceleration is still heavily concentrated in goods and energy-related costs rather than reflecting an equally broad-based increase across the services sector.

Overall, the data points to significant inflationary shock in Italy, largely driven by surging energy costs but increasingly spilling over into food and transportation prices.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Eurozone Q3 GDP beats expectations but the growth surprise comes with a catch
item.description:
• Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +0.4% vs +0.2% q/q expected
  • Prior +0.6%
  • Eurozone Q3 preliminary GDP +1.3% vs +1.1% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.2%

Well, well, well. Would you look at that. The euro area economy has managed to pull a rabbit out of the hat, delivering a better-than-expected Q3 GDP reading at first glance. But before we start popping the champagne, there's a catch or two worth considering when you look at the details.

To start, quarterly growth did still slow down to 0.4% in the third quarter - down from 0.6% in the second quarter. So while the headline surprise is encouraging, the underlying momentum isn't quite as impressive as it might seem.

And when you drill deeper into the details, that is when things start to get a bit more interesting.

Of note, Ireland leads the pack with a whopping 5.5% quarterly expansion in Q3. Having said that, Ireland has a knack for notoriously volatile GDP figures in the past year and that always warrants some caution. The expansion here was primarily driven by strong activity in multinational-dominated industries, specifically information and communication and manufacturing.

For some context, Ireland's headline growth figure is often a distorted gauge of domestic economic health. That is because it is heavily influenced by contract manufacturing and global profits of multinational corporations that largely flow back to foreign shareholders rather than translating directly into local living standards.

Besides that, Spain continues to punch above its weight with 0.6% growth while the Netherlands also posted a respectable 0.6% increase.

Elsewhere though? The picture isn't so pretty.

Germany managed just 0.2% growth, Italy stagnated at 0.0%, and France even contracted by 0.1%. Now, that's hardly an endorsement of economic resilience across the biggest economies in the region.

So, what does this mean for the ECB?

We've seen inflation pressures heating up in France and Spain today even as the growth picture remains rather uneven. Meanwhile, German state inflation readings offered some relief but the broader concern remains that higher energy costs would eventually feed through to prices while weighing on economic activity.

And that is precisely the kind of stagflationary squeeze policymakers would want to avoid at this juncture.

So the real question now is whether the euro area can maintain its growth momentum as higher prices are going to squeeze households and businesses more and more in the months ahead. The latest report today might suggest that growth conditions are holding up a little bit better than feared, but whether that remains the case heading into Q4 will be a different story altogether.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold gets hit again by forced liquidations as equity losses mount; fundamental outlook increasingly positive
item.description:
Gold came under renewed pressure yesterday as another selloff in equities weighed on precious metals. Gold has been tightly correlated with the stock market recently, with the latest losses seemingly driven by investors liquidating positions to cover losses elsewhere in their portfolios.

Chart: You can see the correlation between the Nasdaq (blue line) and gold (candlesticks)

To understand the mechanics, imagine that an investment fund holds stocks, gold and government bonds. Some stocks suddenly crash, and the fund suffers losses on leveraged positions. The fund may need to raise cash to meet margin calls, reduce leverage or satisfy investor redemptions. Rather than selling only the assets that caused the losses, it may sell whatever it can liquidate quickly. Gold is particularly useful in this situation because it is highly liquid and can be sold quickly.

The main drivers like real yields have been actually pointing to higher gold prices. In fact, real yields fell significantly as inflation expectations remain roughly unchanged given the increase in oil prices, while nominal Treasury yields fell as the losses in the stock market triggered a flight to safety.

We can also see the unusual divergence between spot gold and the ETFs holdings in the chart below. Generally speaking, spot prices lead ETFs inflows and outflows, but in this case, I think it’s technical factors capping the upside in gold, not fundamental ones.

Once the artificial selling stops weighing on gold, we could see a strong and quick rebound. We are also approaching a generally favourable seasonal period between December and January. The hard part is timing. Traders could lean on key technical levels or wait for a fundamental catalyst. Potential catalysts include a breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations, dovish Fed comments or weaker US data.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that gold(CFD contract) has extended the losses and it’s approaching the major support zone around the 3,885 level. If the price gets there, we can expect the buyers to step in, with a defined risk below the major upward trendline, to position for a rally into new record highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break below the trendline to increase the bearish bets into the 3,500 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we can see the price broke below the minor upward trendline yesterday and extended the drop as the sellers increased the bearish bets into the 3,885 level. If we get a rebound before the 3,885 level, we can expect the sellers to lean on the downward trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to open the door for new highs and position for a rally into the 4,400 level next.

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum on this timeframe. We can expect the sellers to continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to position for a rebound into the major downward trendline. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

UPCOMING CATALYSTS

Todaywe conclude the week with the US Employment Cost Index.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: German state inflation cools in October, but will that ease the ECB's headache?
item.description:
The state readings released around the same time:

  • Bavaria September CPI +2.8% vs +3.2% y/y prior
  • Saxony September CPI +2.9% vs +3.3% y/y prior
  • North Rhine Westphalia September CPI +2.7% vs +3.3% y/y prior
  • Baden Wuerttemberg September CPI +2.6% vs +2.9% y/y prior

After the acceleration in September, headline inflation is seen cooling back a little in German states. While base effects are part of the reason, the re-implementation of specific energy tax reductions and fuel discounts enacted at the start of the month are arguably also playing a part here.

So, that is leading to cooler price pressures overall but still relatively elevated when compared to the months before this.

Putting the estimates together, it offers an indication that German inflation is set to decline at the national level as well. Headline annual inflation is expected to drop to 3.0% in October from 3.3% last month, with the state readings above pointing to a modest likelihood that we might even see a reading below the 3% mark.

In any case, just keep in mind though that the state readings aren't a perfect proxy for the national figure. There can still be some deviation when the preliminary numbers are released later. However, they have historically been a useful gauge and today's readings arguably point to some downside risk to the 3.0% consensus, with a national CPI reading around 2.9% now looking quite plausible.

For the ECB, the readings here will just complicate things further as the economic backdrop is reflecting flagging growth conditions amid the risk of price pressures accelerating further. While German inflation may not have jumped in October, there are signs elsewhere that inflation is starting to spread more broadly as seen with France and Spain earlier.

So, that will just keep the pressure on policymakers to act again in December while having to consider if doing too much could risk sending the euro area economy over the edge.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Italy Q3 preliminary GDP +0.0% vs +0.1% q/q expected
item.description:
• Prior +0.2%
  • GDP Y/Y +0.8% vs +0.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +1.0%

Italy's economy unexpectedly stalled in the third quarter of 2026, with GDP remaining unchanged q/q, following 0.2% growth in the previous quarter. On an annual basis, GDP increased by 0.8%, pointing to a relatively modest pace of economic expansion.

On the supply side, services and agriculture provided positive contributions to growth, while industrial activity declined. The weakness in industry remains a concern, particularly given the sector's importance to Italy's export-oriented economy.

On the demand side, domestic demand, including changes in inventories, supported economic activity, while net foreign demand acted as a drag. This suggests that domestic spending continues to provide some resilience, but external demand and trade flows remain a source of weakness.

The carry-over growth rate for 2026 stands at 0.8% on a calendar-adjusted basis. This means that even if GDP remains unchanged in the fourth quarter, annual growth would still be around 0.8%, although the final annual figure may differ due to the three additional working days in 2026 compared with 2025.

The report is mildly negative for the growth outlook. The stagnation in quarterly GDP, combined with industrial weakness and a negative contribution from net exports, highlights structural growth challenges. Domestic demand remains the main source of resilience, but the economy is still struggling to generate broader-based growth.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Germany Q3 preliminary GDP +0.2% vs +0.1% q/q expected
item.description:
• Prior +0.3%
  • GDP Y/Y +1.2% vs 1.1% expected
  • Prior +1.0%

Germany's economy expanded by 0.2% q/q in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data from Destatis, extending the recovery seen in the first half of the year. GDP increased by 1.3% y/y in price-adjusted terms, or 1.2% when adjusted for both prices and calendar effects.

However, the underlying details point to a loss of momentum, with the recovery becoming increasingly uneven. Consumer spending made a modest positive contribution, suggesting that domestic demand is holding up, but investment declined, highlighting continued weakness in business activity.

Meanwhile, exports, which provided a significant boost to growth during the first half of the year, lost momentum in Q3. This is particularly relevant for Germany, given its heavy reliance on external demand and the importance of its manufacturing and export sectors.

Overall, the report suggests that Germany's economic recovery is losing some steam. Growth is still positive, although the weaker performance of investment and exports raises questions about how sustainable the recovery will be heading into the final quarter of the year considering all the headwinds from tightening financial conditions and geopolitical shocks.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: Stocks stumble as AI fears spook markets, Italy and Spain lead losses
item.description:
European stocks are opening mostly lower today as the risk-off mood continues to reverberate across global markets. The renewed selloff in tech shares is not helping, after Amazon's earnings added another layer of anxiety surrounding AI spending. Here are the opening changes:

  • Eurostoxx -0.8%
  • Germany DAX -0.3%
  • France CAC 40 flat
  • UK FTSE +0.3%
  • Spain IBEX -1.0%
  • Italy FTSE MIB -1.2%

Italian and Spanish stocks are leading the declines, with the latter continuing its miserable run this week and threatening fresh three-month lows again. The struggle in Spain largely comes amid the fallout from Brazil's election shock, particularly among banking stocks and other companies with significant exposure to the country - namely Santander, Telefonica, and Mapfre.

As for the broader market mood, the more worrying development is that the tech selloff is showing little signs of letting up.

After Alphabet earlier in the week, Amazon is the latest big name to disappoint investors this week. The company saw earnings miss while hefty AI spending commitments only served to reignite concerns about whether all those billions that are being poured into AI will eventually deliver the returns investors are hoping for.

The anxiety and nervousness is also reflected in US futures today, with S&P 500 futures down 1.0% and Nasdaq futures down 2.1% currently. And so that leaves European investors with a rather uncomfortable backdrop heading into the final trading day of October.

There will be some economic data to digest in Europe, with GDP and inflation numbers on the agenda. So, just keep an eye out for that as those readings could add another wrinkle to the outlook for ECB policy heading into December.

Howeer, the big question for broader markets now is whether Wall Street can find some stability later today. With AI spending fears haunting markets ahead of Halloween, it might take more than a few reassuring earnings headlines to restore confidence.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Spain Q3 GDP growth slows slightly but it's the inflation problem that should worry the ECB
item.description:
• Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +0.6% vs +0.6% q/q expected
  • Prior +0.7%
  • Spain Q3 preliminary GDP +2.7% vs +2.7% y/y expected
  • Prior +2.6%

It is the preliminary report, so there aren't much details to work with here besides the headline figures above.

The quarterly figure does show a bit of a slowdown in Spanish economic growth in the third quarter, albeit marginally. And among the bigger names in the euro area, Spain is still very much punching above its weight in carrying the more optimistic banner for the region.

The only issue is that inflation pressures in Spain is also starting to get out of hand. Headline annual inflation is bordering on 5% in October with core annual inflation holding above 3%. Those numbers are way beyond what the ECB would be comfortable with, running above their 2% price target.

The Spanish GDP report here isn't something to spook markets. But a mild slowdown if coupled with troubling performances in France and perhaps Germany later, that could really ramp up talk of stagflation risks in the euro area especially when paired with the inflation numbers today.

Traders might still lean more favourably on inflation risks prompting the ECB to act in December. But if growth conditions continue to suffer, it might only be a matter of time before the narrative shifts and the focus turns to stagflation risks instead. So, just be wary of that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Spain inflation remains stubbornly high near 5% as the ECB headache gets worse
item.description:
• Spain October preliminary CPI +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%
  • Spain October preliminary HICP +4.9% vs +4.9% y/y expected
  • Prior +5.0%

Spanish inflation continues to hover around 5% in October, as the preliminary estimates continue to paint a rather uncomfortable picture for the most part. Headline annual inflation remains steady at 4.9% while the harmonised reading eased marginally to 4.9% as well. So, that's not saying a lot after the run higher in the past few months amid a surge energy prices due to the Middle East conflict.

And with higher oil prices continuing to stick, that will certainly add to the inflation headache in Q4.

Looking at the details, core annual inflation is seen at 3.1% - unchanged compared to September. But at this level, it is still well above what the ECB would be comfortable with as price pressures continue to pull away from the 2% target.

Alongside the earlier report from France, this just continues to reaffirm that the inflation monster is getting bigger and more threatening for the central bank. But at the same time, flagging economic growth conditions will just mean that stagflation risks are also on the rise.

So, that is quite a troubling spot for policymakers to be in as they have to try and deal with price pressures before they get out of hand while avoiding sending the broader economy off a cliff. Tough.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France inflation heats up again in October, leaving the ECB caught between a rock and a hard place
item.description:
• France October preliminary CPI +3.4% vs +3.2% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.1%
  • France October preliminary HICP +3.8% vs +3.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.4%

French inflation is seen accelerating again in October, as the preliminary estimates show headline annual inflation climbing to its highest since December 2023. Yowza.

The main culprit is once again energy prices, as that continues to fuel much of the headline price increase. No pun intended. Of note, energy price inflation was up 24.1% annually in October compared to 21.3% in the month before.

The detailed breakdown shows food price inflation softening slightly to 1.2% in October but services inflation is seen picking up further to 2.7% from 2.4% in the month before. The latter is a real issue as it signals that higher energy prices are starting to spill over more broadly, and that will in turn feed into core inflation as well.

It's not a good look if you're the ECB. France is already struggling economically, not to mention with fiscal headwinds growing stronger by the day. And with inflation pressures starting to heat up as well, that is making for a very stagflationary outlook for Europe's second-largest economy.

For the central bank, this is their biggest issue and risk to tightening policy further. That is especially the case as French bonds are also coming under heavy pressure amid fiscal worries and that could threaten to blow over to the rest of the euro area as well.

It's really a case of damned if you do, damned if you don't for the ECB.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: German import prices surge at fastest pace in nearly four years as energy costs bite
item.description:
• Germany September import prices +2.1% vs +1.8% m/m expected
  • Prior +1.0%
  • Germany September import prices +10.4% vs +10.3% y/y expected
  • Prior +8.3%

Just when Germany thought it had enough economic headaches to deal with, here's another one to add to the pile. This time, the inflation monster is making quite the comeback through the back door.

German import prices for September are seen rosing at their fastest annual pace since November 2022, with the monthly increase also coming in hotter than expected. And surprise, surprise. Not. It is energy that is once again doing much of the damage.

Imported energy prices surged by a whopping 61.8% compared to a year ago, with electricity prices almost doubling (+96.2%) compared to the year before. The US-Iran conflict is definitely leaving its mark on Germany's import bill and businesses aren't exactly getting much breathing room elsewhere either.

Prices for intermediate goods rose 11.1% annually, including a 37.9% increase in copper and 23.4% rise in aluminium. And even if you strip out energy prices, import prices were still up by 5.5% year-on-year in September.

So, what does this tell us?

To start, the details suggest that Germany's imported inflation problem isn't just about expensive oil and gas prices. Higher input costs are spreading across industrial supply chains and that could potentially squeeze manufacturers' margins at a time when the economy can ill afford another setback.

And this also spells trouble for the ECB. Now, import prices aren't the same as consumer prices of course. However, sustained increases in energy and production costs could eventually filter through to households, depending on how much businesses can pass those costs along.

All in all, this will just be another anecdote in reaffirming the prospects of another ECB rate hike in December - especially with markets already pricing in roughly 61% odds of such a move at this juncture.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda tries to play down inflation victory declaration, says it will be up to the government to call that
item.description:
Further remarks on the day by Ueda:

  • Not yet able to decalre that inflation target has been achieved
  • We think it is mportant for inflation to stably and sustainably hold around 2%
  • BOJ not planning to make a formal declaration at some point that price target has been achieved
  • It is up to government to declare the end of deflation
  • Will not comment on whether the joint accord with the government will be revised or not
  • For now, cannot ignore risk of inflation overshooting
  • Overshooting risks have not necessarily increased compared with a month ago

As a reminder, it was the BOJ outlook report earlier that noted that underlying inflation is generally consistent with the 2% target and is expected to stay there. And Ueda also reaffirmed that view with his earlier comments here. Alongside revising their inflation forecasts higher, it is more or less a victory declaration on inflation. Even Ueda himself said that all members on the board agreed that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target now.

But yet, Ueda wants to play this down instead of use it as a springboard to push more rate hikes. And that says a lot about the current appetite of the BOJ to be more proactive in taking action.

As much as we want to think the BOJ has changed and is becoming more bold, Ueda is serving up a timely reminder here that they would still very much prefer to err on the side of caution and move more slowly instead. Another rate hike in December is very much still up in the air.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ governor Ueda says will stick to rate hike path in response to latest macro developments
item.description:
In case you missed it, the BOJ left its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% in a 8-1 vote earlier today. And while the decision in itself was widely expected, the central bank finally moved to declare victory on inflation after a hard-fought battle for more than a decade.

Ueda is now following up on that decision and is arguing that the board is sharing a unanimous view on prices at this juncture. His comments:

  • Japan's economy expected to continue growing moderately
  • Underlying inflation at level generally consistent with 2% price stability target, expected to remain at around that level
  • All members agreed that underlying inflation has reached 2% target
  • Cannot condone underlying inflation from becoming higher
  • BOJ will continue to raise policy rate and adjust degree of monetary easing in response to economic activity, prices, and financial developments
  • Will consider adjustment of timing, pace on monetary policy while looking at likelihood of achieving baseline scenarios to the economic, price outlook
  • Need to monitor risks, financial environment and impact on economy, prices a little more (when asked on why the BOJ chose to hold today)
  • However, more important than ever that underlying inflation is not allowed to overshoot 2% target

Well, his comments are certainly leaning more towards the hawkish side but yet the BOJ is not willing to take any action. That pretty much says it all.

The balance of risks has certainly shifted, with policymakers now underscoring the necessity to not let inflation get out of hand. And so the only question now is how willing is the BOJ to step up its game and walk the talk instead of just talking the talk.

Ueda also adds that they will want to be more proactive and will "promptly" adjust policy to steer inflation to 2% rather than "waiting passively". But again, actions speak louder than words.

December remains very much in play but it is clear that the BOJ wants to keep their options open. The only issue though in waiting too long is that they might miss their timing, even more so when Japan prime minister Takaichi is going to have another opportunity to reshape the board next year. And that could very well make it even tougher for the BOJ to pursue any further tightening measures.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France's economy contracts in Q3 as growth troubles pile up for the ECB
item.description:
• France Q3 preliminary GDP -0.1% vs +0.1% q/q expected
  • Prior 0.0%
  • France Q3 preliminary GDP % vs +0.3% y/y expected
  • Prior +0.5%

Ouch. That's a notable miss as French GDP shrinks in Q3 this year. That follows from the stagnation in Q2 and a 0.2% contraction in Q1, not exactly the sort of economic performance one would hope for from Europe's second-largest economy.

Looking at the breakdown, household consumption actually improved in rising to 0.4% from 0.2% previously. However, investment remained a major weak spot in falling by 0.6% after a 0.5% decline in the quarter before this.

The big drag came from exports, slumping by 1.7% and reversing a 2.8% increase in the previous quarter. That saw net trade subtract 0.6% from growth, although inventory changes provided a 0.4% cushion and domestic demand added the final 0.1%.

So, what does this mean for the ECB?

Well, the latest figures highlight an economy that is largely struggling amid weak investment and soft external demand. And with France already facing significant fiscal challenges, there's limited room for government spending to provide much support.

So, that doesn't really change all too much for the central bank as much of this sentiment is already captured by the bond market. The French numbers will strengthen the argument for caution on further tightening, although policymakers will remain more concerned about price stability at the balance.

But if similar weakness starts showing up elsewhere in the euro area, then the case for further rate hikes will become more and more difficult to justify heading into next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What is spooking markets as stocks, Treasury yields and gold all fall ahead of European trading?
item.description:
It looks like Halloween is coming a day early for markets with investors getting quite the fright already as we look to wrap up the trading week. Both stocks and Treasury yields are falling together, with gold also struggling to catch a bid. That's a rather spooky combination to deal with.

So, what exactly is driving markets into this scary situation?

Well, the latest earnings from Amazon overnight have only added another skeleton to the closet after the company's massive AI spending bill overshadowed impressive cloud growth. Amazon shares are down 7% in after-hours trading, and that follows from the beating that tech shares took yesterday after Alphabet reignited fears of AI spending in the day before.

US futures are being dragged sharply lower today, with Nasdaq futures down 1.8% currently. And that is setting up a rather ominous backdrop ahead of European trading today.

But beyond the selling in tech, there's something else about the broader market moves worth noting. Why are Treasury yields continuing to fall when inflation risks remain elevated? And why exactly aren't lower yields doing much to offer support for tech stocks?

Perhaps the answer lies in the darker story brewing beneath the AI boom.

For all the excitement surrounding AI technology, investors are starting to question just how much money companies need to throw at it before seeing meaningful returns. And Alphabet and Amazon's latest results this week are hardly going to put those worries to bed.

And as AI credit risks continue to attract scrutiny, falling Treasury yields may be telling us something about investors seeking safety rather than celebrating lower borrowing costs.

As for gold, the inability for the precious metal to capitalise on the negative risk mood adds another twist to the overall picture. That could reflect month-end positioning or even liquidity pressures as stocks are being hurt badly while the bond market is responding more to safety flows rather than inflation risks. The latter is still very much in play as oil prices continue to stay more elevated this week.

So, where does that leave us ahead of European trading today?

It's a rather poor risk backdrop overall and one that could get uglier at any point in time. For me, I'd be watching whether the tech selloff spills over into broader equities more profoundly and whether Treasury yields will continue to fall alongside stocks. The latter will be a particularly worrying sight for broader markets if so.

As things stand, the real fright for markets may not be that the AI boom is running out of steam but that investors are finally starting to question the price of keeping it all going.

"It's all a fugazi. It's a wazi. It's a woozy. It's fairy dust. It doesn't exist. It's never landed. It is no matter. It's not on the elemental chart. It's not real."

Said nobody. ;)

item.title: BOJ declares inflation victory but still won't budge on rates, so what's the hold-up?
item.description:
If you think back to a decade ago, the BOJ being able to even see the path to reach the inflation target was very much a pipedream. Yet, here we are today. The central bank finally gets to declare victory on inflation. That must mean champagne all around, surely? Well, not quite.

As it would seem, getting to the finish line and convincing policymakers to do something about it are two very different things.

The BOJ kept its policy rate unchanged today at 1.25% in a 8-1 vote, with board member Takata dissenting in playing the role as the lone hawk again. He called for a 25 bps rate hike to 1.50% but the rest of the board wasn't having any of it. So, what's the story here?

The most interesting bit of the meeting decision today is that the BOJ now says that underlying inflation has reached a level broadly consistent with its 2% target. Policymakers also expect inflation to remain around there as we move forward. So, that is quite a milestone after more than a decade of trying to get inflation sustainably back on track.

Adding to that, the central bank also raised its core inflation forecast for fiscal year 2027 to 2.6% from 2.4% previously.

So if inflation is already where policymakers want it to be, what's stopping them from moving faster?

As it turns out, the overwhelming majority of the board clearly still prefers a more measured approach. Having just raised interest rates in September, there's little appetite to rush another move while assessing how previous tightening is feeding through to the economy. How typical of the BOJ, eh?

But in the bigger picture, I would argue that there is the political headache to consider.

Japan prime minister Takaichi's two board appointees, namely Asada and Sato, already voted against the rate hike in September. And that will serve as a reminder that getting further tightening through the board might not be quite so straightforward, even though the central bank has already declared victory on inflation.

Looking to next year, things could get even trickier and more challenging for the BOJ. Takaichi will have the opportunity to nominate replacements for two more board members in 2027. And if those appointments lean similarly dovish (which they likely will *coughs*), Ueda could find himself facing a more divided committee.

Even with today's signal, traders are pricing roughly 57% odds of another 25 bps rate hike in December. That is hardly a convincing endorsement of the next move, let alone any real confidence in the BOJ stepping up their tightening pace next year.

As for Ueda's press conference later, I would expect him to reiterate that further tightening remains on the table while keeping the timing deliberately vague. That'd be very on-brand of him. If anything, just watch for whether he puts more emphasis on the inflation milestone or the need to assess growth, wages and financial conditions.

But unless he offers something more definitive, I suspect markets will be left with much the same question heading into December.

After such a long battle, the BOJ has finally managed to tick the inflation box. However, now comes the harder part of getting everyone on board with what happens next.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

It said about $2.5 billion has been frozen, but gave no figure for losses or a timeline for reopening.

More than $1 billion, mostly ether, was reported to be beyond reach. Binance’s BNB token fell 8.6% to near $694 and bitcoin slipped to around $77,700.

item.title: BoJ declares underlying inflation at 2% target, lifts FY2027 price forecast as rates held
item.description:
The meeting delivered almost everything hawks had looked for: the 2% declaration, upside price risks, a higher inflation forecast and a dissent in favour of a hike, with no dovish split. That should support the yen near 157.8 per dollar, push short-dated JGB yields higher and firm December hike pricing from around 80%. Oil sits at the centre of the forecasts. The bank assumes Dubai crude falls from about $105 to $70, so a sustained rise in prices tied to the Iran conflict would add to the upside risk to inflation. Faster ETF sales add modest supply for Japanese equities from 2027, though a 43-year horizon keeps the annual impact small.

-The Bank of Japan has all but declared victory over deflation, and its own forecasts now say inflation is the bigger risk.

Summary:

  • , 0630 GMT,  in an 8-1 vote; Takata proposed a hike to 1.5%
  • The Outlook Report says underlying inflation is generally consistent with the 2% target and expected to stay there
  • Risks to prices are skewed to the upside, while risks to activity are generally balanced
  • FY2027 core CPI forecast raised to 2.6% from 2.4%; FY2026 unchanged at 2.5%, FY2028 at 2.0%
  • Real GDP is seen at 0.7% in FY2026 and FY2027 and 0.8% in FY2028
  • ETF sales will rise to about 860 billion yen a year from January 2027, cutting the disposal timeline to about 43 years from about 112

The Bank of Japan said underlying inflation is now generally consistent with its 2% price stability target, a long-awaited declaration that strengthens the case for further rate hikes. It kept its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% on Friday.

In its quarterly Outlook Report, the central bank said underlying consumer price inflation is at a level broadly in line with the target and is expected to stay around there. It pointed to a persistent sense of labour shortage, an interaction between rising wages and prices, and medium- to long-term inflation expectations of about 2%. The bank described the risks to prices as skewed to the upside. It warned that inflation expectations could rise and push underlying inflation above target as firms increasingly lift wages and prices.

The board’s median forecast for core inflation, which excludes fresh food, was raised to 2.6% for fiscal 2027 from 2.4% previously, reflecting the rise in crude oil prices since the summer. The fiscal 2026 forecast was unchanged at 2.5%, and fiscal 2028 stayed at 2.0%. The bank expects core inflation to rise to a level clearly above 2% in the first half of the projection period, driven by oil, higher prices for semiconductors and other items, and a weaker yen. It then sees inflation easing toward around 2% as the effect of high oil prices fades. Its projections assume Dubai crude falls from around $105 a barrel to around $70 by the end of the forecast period, and they exclude the effect of a proposed cut to the consumption tax on food.

Growth forecasts were little changed, with real GDP seen expanding 0.7% in fiscal 2026 and 2027 and 0.8% in fiscal 2028. The bank expects the economy to keep growing at a slower pace this fiscal year, as higher energy costs linked to the Middle East weigh on activity, supported by government measures and AI-related demand.

The policy board voted 8-1 to hold rates. Board member Hajime Takata dissented, proposing a hike to 1.5% on the grounds that with underlying inflation at target, the bank should speed up moves toward the neutral rate. No board member dissented in favour of a cut, removing a risk flagged ahead of the meeting.

The bank also unanimously agreed to more than double the pace of its ETF sales from January 2027, to about 860 billion yen a year on a book value basis from about 330 billion yen. That would shorten the time needed to sell its holdings to about 43 years from around 112.

Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later on Friday, 0630 GMT,  will be watched for signals on whether the 2% declaration opens the door to a hike in December. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BoJ keeps policy rate unchanged at 1.25%, as expected
item.description:
BoJ keeps policy rate unchanged at 1.25%, as expected

The vote leans hawkish. The dissent the market feared, a call for a cut, didn’t happen, and the only objection came from a member pushing for a hike now. That should support the yen near 157.8 per dollar and keep December pricing, about 80% going in, firmly in place. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields may edge higher. The faster ETF sales add modest supply to Japanese equities from 2027, a mild headwind for the Nikkei. The final read will depend on the Outlook Report and Ueda’s tone, with oil-driven inflation pressure keeping the case for tightening alive.

---

  • BOJ seen lifting rates to 1.50% in December as 69% of economists expect a Q4 hike
  • BOJ reportedly may upgrade inflation forecast, hold rates steady at next week's meeting

---

The Bank of Japan stood still as expected, but the only voice of dissent wanted to go faster, and the yen bears’ nightmare of a dovish split never showed up.

Summary:

  • The BoJ held its short-term policy rate at around 1.25% in an 8-1 vote
  • Takata dissented, proposing a hike to 1.5% on the view that underlying inflation has reached the 2% target
  • No dovish dissent emerged, removing a key yen risk flagged before the meeting
  • The board unanimously raised the pace of ETF sales to about 860 billion yen a year (book value) from about 330 billion
  • The new ETF pace takes effect in January 2027; J-REIT sales are unchanged
  • Focus turns to the Outlook Report and Ueda’s press conference

The Bank of Japan kept its short-term policy rate unchanged at 1.25% on Friday, as widely expected. The decision came with a hawkish dissent and a sharp increase in the pace at which the central bank will sell its holdings of exchange-traded funds.

The policy board voted 8-1 to keep guiding the uncollateralised overnight call rate at around 1.25%. Board member Hajime Takata voted against and proposed raising the rate to around 1.5%. He argued that with underlying consumer price inflation having reached the bank’s 2% price stability target, the situation had moved into a new phase. In his view, the bank needs to speed up the pace of bringing its policy rate closer to the neutral rate, so that it can respond nimbly. His proposal was defeated by a majority vote.

The vote removes one of the main risks flagged ahead of the meeting. Two board members who opposed September’s rate hike had been seen as possible dissenters in favour of a cut. Analysts had warned that such a move could undercut a hawkish message and weaken the yen. Instead, the only dissent came from the hawkish side.

The board also voted unanimously to more than double the pace of its ETF sales. The bank began selling the funds in January this year at about 330 billion yen a year on a book value basis, equivalent to around 0.05% of market trading value. From January 2027, it will sell at about 0.1% of trading value, or roughly 860 billion yen a year on a book value basis. On a market value basis, that equates to about 2.5 trillion yen a year. The bank said the sales had proceeded smoothly without a major market impact, while trading in the stock market had expanded. It retained the option to adjust or suspend sales temporarily in response to market conditions. It left its sales of Japanese real estate investment trusts unchanged at about 5 billion yen a year.

Markets were pricing about an 80% chance of a hike in December going into the meeting. Attention now turns to the quarterly Outlook Report, which analysts expect to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%. Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later in the afternoon will be watched for any signal on the timing of the next move.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:
The yen and short-dated Japanese government bond yields are where any surprise will show, with USD/JPY near 157.8 going into the release. Because a hold is fully priced, the market reaction will come from the language and the vote. A hawkish package would likely strengthen the yen and lift two-year yields. A dovish split could trigger renewed yen selling. Oil prices remain a background factor: Brent’s run of monthly gains strengthens the case for tighter policy because energy feeds directly into Japan’s import costs. Japanese bank stocks tend to benefit from signals of higher rates, while exporters could feel pressure from a firmer yen.

---

The Bank of Japan will almost certainly stand still today, so watch what it says, who votes against it and how Ueda chooses his words.

Summary:

  • The BoJ decision is due shortly, with no fixed release time; a hold at 1.25% is widely expected
  • Markets price about an 80% chance of a December hike
  • Analysts expect the Outlook Report to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached 2%
  • Dissent risk runs both ways: two members could call for a cut, while another may push for a hike
  • Ueda’s press conference language will be key for December signals
  • Tokyo core CPI matched forecasts at 2.6%, output beat expectations and retail sales disappointed

The Bank of Japan is due to announce its policy decision shortly. The central bank is widely expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25%, and markets are focused on any signal that a hike is coming in December.

The decision has no fixed release time, but it typically lands around midday in Tokyo. A hold is almost fully expected, with traders pricing virtually no chance of a move at this meeting following hikes in June and September. Markets now see about an 80% chance of a December increase, up from earlier in the month, and a hawkish tone is widely anticipated.

Three elements will shape the market reaction. The first is the quarterly Outlook Report, in which analysts expect the board to effectively declare that underlying inflation has reached the bank’s 2% target. That would mark a shift from pushing inflation higher to keeping it stable. Policymakers may also nudge up their inflation forecasts as higher oil prices feed through to consumer prices.

The second is the vote. Two board members opposed the September hike and could dissent in favour of a cut. That would undercut a hawkish message and weigh on the yen. Another member may push in the opposite direction and propose a hike.

The third is Governor Kazuo Ueda’s press conference later in the afternoon. Any shift from saying rates are decided meeting by meeting toward language pointing to the next meeting would likely be read as a strong December signal.

The morning’s data gave policymakers a mixed picture. Core inflation in Tokyo, which excludes fresh food, came in at 2.6% in October, in line with forecasts and above target. Factory output rose more than expected in September, and manufacturers lifted their October production plans sharply, while retail sales fell short of expectations.

The yen has held steady near 157.8 per dollar ahead of the announcement. A clear 2% declaration, a firm Ueda and a hawkish dissent would likely support the currency and push short-dated Japanese government bond yields higher. A dovish split or a cautious tone could trim December expectations and weaken the yen. 

  Bank of Japan Governor Ueda press conference will follow at 0630 GMT.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: (Some good news!) Treasuries rally as AI selloff drives flight to safety, 10-year yield at one-month low
item.description:
Lower Treasury yields ease financing costs across the curve, offering some relief to rate-sensitive sectors and to the AI firms whose borrowing has worried investors. That makes the bond rally partly self-correcting for the very stress that triggered it. A softer dollar supports Asian currencies and commodities priced in dollars. Oil remains the main threat to the rally: with Brent heading for a fourth straight monthly gain, any escalation in the Iran conflict could quickly revive inflation fears and push yields back up. The BoJ decision later today is the next test, and a hawkish surprise could firm the yen against a softer dollar.

---

  • Vessel on fire in Strait of Hormuz after incident near Oman, cause "unknown" (LOL)

Stocks slammed:

  • Earnings bloodbath: Intel crashes over 22%, Amazon over 12%. What's coming next?

$6bn stolen in a hack:

But ... at least Treasuries are bouncing!

---

The AI selloff finally gave bond investors something to cheer, though with oil still climbing and central banks still hawkish, the celebration may be brief.

Summary:

  • The US 10-year Treasury yield fell to around 4.90% and the 30-year to about 5.26%, both one-month lows
  • The rally was driven by safe-haven buying amid renewed selling in AI stocks after Alphabet, Amazon and Intel results
  • Strategists noted that AI concerns lowered yields and softened the dollar, unlike energy-driven risk-off episodes
  • The dollar index edged down to around 101.8 but is on track for a second straight monthly gain
  • The yen held near 157.8 ahead of the BoJ, with about an 80% chance of a December hike priced
  • ANZ’s Khoon Goh sees this week’s central bank pauses as temporary, with more hikes possible in 2027

US Treasuries rallied as a fresh wave of selling in artificial intelligence stocks sent investors in search of safety, Reuters reported on Friday. The rally pushed benchmark yields to their lowest levels in more than a month and weighed on the US dollar.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell to around 4.90%, while the 30-year yield dropped to about 5.26%, both at more than one-month lows. Bond yields move inversely to prices, so the declines reflect strong buying of US government debt.

The rally was triggered by renewed concern over the cost of the AI boom. Results from Alphabet earlier in the week revived worries about AI spending and pulled broader stock markets lower. Disappointing results from Amazon and Intel after Thursday’s close added to the pressure. As equities sold off, safe-haven bonds became more attractive.

Strategists noted that the pattern differed from recent bouts of market stress. An energy-driven risk-off episode would typically lift the dollar and push yields higher. This time, one Singapore-based strategist said, the US-focused AI concerns came with lower Treasury yields and a softer or subdued dollar. That suggests investors are treating the AI selloff as a US growth and earnings risk rather than an inflation shock.

The lower yields weighed on the greenback. The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against a basket of major peers, edged down to around 101.8, although it remained on course for a second consecutive monthly gain.

Elsewhere in currency markets, the yen was steady near 157.8 per dollar ahead of the Bank of Japan’s policy decision. The central bank is expected to hold rates at 1.25% with a hawkish tone, and markets are pricing about an 80% chance of a hike in December. The euro was flat near $1.12 after touching its lowest level since May 2025 in the previous session. The Australian dollar held around $0.70, on track for a 1.2% gain in October.

The relief for bond markets may prove limited. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand all held rates steady this week, but have signalled their tightening cycles are not over, with energy prices near multi-month highs. Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, described the current pauses as temporary. He said the risk heading into 2027 is that elevated inflation could bring even more hikes. Brent crude is on track for its fourth straight monthly gain, the longest run in more than two years.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Amazon and Intel results deepen worries over AI boom costs as tech, chip stocks slide
item.description:
The after-hours moves pointed to a weak start for Nasdaq futures in Asia, with semiconductor and AI infrastructure names most exposed in regional trade, including Asian chip and hardware suppliers. The funding angle may matter more than the earnings misses. Rising Big Tech debt issuance and pressure on leveraged AI cloud firms tie directly into concerns about tightening financial conditions and AI-related credit supply. If the selling deepens, investors may rotate toward the AI chip leaders that analysts see as less exposed to PC weakness, rather than out of the sector entirely.

---

Earlier:

  • Amazon Q3 operating profit beats estimates, but EPS misses and Q4 guidance looks soft. Share price drops.
  • Intel beats Q3 profit forecasts, but weak Q4 guidance and PC outlook weigh. Share price drops.
  • Intel shares tumble around 15%. The narrative is --> weak Q4 guidance overshadows Q3 profit beat
  • Earnings bloodbath: Intel crashes over 22%, Amazon over 12%. What's coming next?

---

The AI build-out is starting to send its bill to everyone, from Big Tech’s balance sheets to the shoppers paying more for their next laptop.

Summary:

  • Amazon fell about 7% after hours on a below-forecast holiday-quarter sales outlook
  • Intel dropped around 18% on weak PC demand and disclosed a $600 million revenue hit from an Israel factory explosion
  • AI cloud stocks CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell 6% to 7%, while HP and Dell sank about 8% and 7%
  • Alphabet and Meta burned cash in the September quarter, and Microsoft launched a $25 billion debt sale
  • Some analysts say Intel’s PC woes don’t necessarily signal trouble for AI-focused chipmakers
  • The semiconductor index is 21% below its June record despite a 60%-plus gain this year

Concern over the cost of the artificial intelligence boom intensified after the US market close on Thursday, Reuters reported. Results from Amazon and Intel suggested the race to build AI infrastructure is weighing not only on technology companies but also on consumers.

Amazon shares fell about 7% in after-hours trading after the company forecast holiday-quarter sales below Wall Street expectations. Reuters said that could signal growing pressure on consumers as inflation picks up. Intel dropped around 18% after flagging near-term weakness across the PC industry, where a shortage of memory chips has pushed up costs and price increases are squeezing demand for devices.

The selling spread well beyond the two companies. AI cloud providers CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren fell roughly 6% to 7% after hours. Alphabet, which had already closed nearly 13% lower following its own results, slipped a further 1.5%. PC makers HP and Dell dropped about 8% and 7%, respectively. In chips, AMD lost 4% and Broadcom 2%. A leveraged exchange-traded fund that offers three times the daily return of the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 9%.

Reuters highlighted a broader shift in how the largest technology firms are funding their spending. Heavy data centre investment has turned once debt-light companies into major borrowers. Alphabet and Meta both burned cash in the September quarter. Microsoft, the only one of the group not to do so, launched a $25 billion debt sale on Thursday. The biggest companies can sustain that spending, but investors have grown more cautious about smaller AI cloud firms borrowing heavily to meet large order backlogs.

Intel also disclosed that an explosion at a factory in Israel forced a two-week shutdown. It expects the incident to cost about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters.

Not everyone sees Intel’s PC troubles as a warning for the wider sector. Some analysts said weakness in personal computers does not necessarily signal problems for chipmakers more closely tied to AI. One trader attributed most of the after-hours chip selling to sentiment spilling over from Intel’s guidance.

The semiconductor index has risen more than 60% this year on shortages of AI-related chips and equipment, but tighter financing conditions have tested that rally over the past month. The index is down 13% from its October high and 21% below its June record.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
